A1.justification: Both PDFs describe LivingSwap and provide readable main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices. The original supplementary sections can be matched across relocation and renumbering, supporting a reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original face-swapping evaluations on FF++ and CineFaceBench, quantitative ablations in Tables 3–4, and additional qualitative experiments in its appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds a quantitative keyframe-selection experiment in Table 5 and an inference-time measurement in Appendix K.

M1.justification: New Appendix D introduces an alternative keyframe-selection procedure using frontal frames with yaw within ±30° and pitch within ±20°. The core architecture, training loss, temporal stitching, and grayscale-keyframe extension already present in v1 remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Training remains based on Face2Face constructed from CelebV-Text and VFHQ; evaluation retains FF++ and CineFaceBench with the same cinematic conditions. The new experiment selects ten existing CineFaceBench cases without expanding dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: Comparator membership in the existing tables and qualitative comparisons is unchanged. New Table 5 adds a separate comparison using Inswapper and fixed-interval LivingSwap as controls for the rule-based keyframe variant, extending comparison participation within this targeted experiment.

E3.justification: Appendix D introduces an evaluation on the ten worst-performing CineFaceBench cases, comparing fixed-interval and orientation-based keyframe selection. Existing benchmark metrics and training budgets are retained. The newly stated 79-frame keyframe interval in Section 5.1 does not establish that existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendix D and Table 5 add a focused analysis of whether frontal-keyframe selection improves difficult cases. Existing analyses of training-data quality, model components, identity variation, imperfect keyframes, and grayscale guidance are retained; the expanded main-text discussion of noisy training pairs summarizes an experiment already in v1 Appendix A.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests for model performance. The added table continues the existing practice of reporting point estimates.

E6.justification: Tables 1–4 and the existing qualitative results are unchanged. New Table 5 reports identity similarity of 0.073 for fixed-interval LivingSwap, 0.240 for rule-based LivingSwap, and 0.224 for Inswapper on ten selected cases; pose error worsens from 3.240 to 3.504 between the LivingSwap variants. Appendix K newly reports 195 seconds for 81 frames. These are additional results, not improvements to the earlier benchmark scores.

T1.justification: The rectified-flow formulation and method equations (1)–(9) retain the same mathematical content. No theorem, proof, formal assumption, or substantive derivation is added or revised.

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution list retain the same novelty, fidelity, temporal-consistency, dataset, benchmark, and approximately 40-fold manual-editing reduction claims. Mentioning CineFaceBench in the revised conclusion repeats an existing contribution.

C2.justification: New Appendix K explicitly qualifies robustness by acknowledging that poor keyframes can bias identity and expression, and identifies slow inference as a practical limitation. Appendix D explains the benefit of frontal keyframes. The earlier discussion of color propagation failures and grayscale mitigation remains present.

D1.justification: Section 5.1 newly specifies fixed-interval keyframes every 79 frames for 81-frame chunks. Appendices D and K provide selection thresholds and inference-resource information: 195 seconds on one H200 with 108 GB memory. Existing training and dataset-construction details and project-access information are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations to Identity-aware and Shape-aware Propagation of Face Editing in Videos, Stitch It in Time, and VividFace. The introduction also refines its discussion of information loss in encoder-derived conditioning. The overall research positioning remains stable.

P1.justification: There are localized grammar corrections and rewrites in the experimental setup, synthetic-data discussion, and conclusion. The appendix gains keyframe-selection and limitations sections, with subsequent sections relettered. Affiliations and acknowledgments are updated, while the overall narrative structure is retained.

P2.justification: Figure 3 is revised with clearer training/inference labels, variable annotations, and depiction of role reversal. Table 5 is added, some table emphasis and captions are corrected, and appendix text reflows around retained figures. Existing qualitative result images are unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 improves transparency through explicit keyframe settings, a targeted selection experiment, and concrete limitations on keyframe reliability and inference speed (Section 5.1; Appendices D and K). These additions help readers assess reproducibility and practical applicability. The gain is limited: the new experiment covers ten selected failures and shows a pose-error tradeoff, while the main benchmark evidence remains unchanged.
